title: What do you want? (Luke 18:31–43)
hook: a blind beggar at Jericho shouts, and Jesus stops the whole procession

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich ruler heard one thing you lack, remembered the Needle's Eye, and was very sorrowful. Your line was what is impossible with men. What did you name as hardest to leave? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Just before Jericho, Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them plainly what's going to happen in Jerusalem: he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, killed, and on the third day rise again. You can't say it much more plainly than that. And Luke adds a sentence that is almost sad: "And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." They have eyes. They've seen everything. And they can't see. Then, on the road outside Jericho, they meet a man who has no eyesight at all.

Luke doesn't name him; Mark calls him Bartimaeus. He's sitting by the roadside, begging, and he hears a crowd going by. What's happening? Jesus of Nazareth is passing. And he shouts, in the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David. That's a title for the promised king. The man who can't see is the one who sees who Jesus is. The people at the front of the crowd tell him to be quiet. "But he cried so much the more." Louder. And then, the line behind our carry: "And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him." A whole crowd on the road to Jerusalem, moving, and it stops. For one beggar. Then a question that sounds almost too obvious: "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?" Isn't it clear? But Jesus asks anyway. He lets the man say it for himself, as a person with a voice and not just a problem. "Lord, that I may receive my sight." The Greek verb can mean see again, and it can mean look up. "And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God." He followed him, up the road to Jerusalem, toward everything the disciples couldn't understand. Look at this week. A beggar at a gate with a name. Faith the size of a seed. One who turned back to say thank you. A kingdom in your midst. Babies carried forward. A ruler who couldn't let go. And now a blind man who could see, a shout that stopped a crowd, and a question: what do you want?
screen: `SON OF DAVID: HE SEES WHO HE IS.`
then, large: `LORD, THAT I MAY RECEIVE MY SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone shouting for help. Settle and breathe. Think about the voices around you asking for help, some loud, some quiet: a friend who keeps mentioning a hard time, a colleague who's struggling, a cause in the news, a family member who calls too often. Which one have you been walking past? Imagine stopping, the whole procession of your day halting, and asking that person: what do you want me to do for you? Then listen for their answer, not yours. If you pray, you can ask for eyes to see who's calling. The bell holds the time.
Bartimaeus. The blind beggar by the road to Jericho, unnamed in Luke but named by Mark, whose shout stopped a whole crowd so Jesus could ask what he wanted.
Your line: Jesus stood still. Today, stop for the person you've been walking past, and ask them what they want. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week on the path.

screen: `DAY 567 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SALVATION CAME TO THIS HOUSE.`

howItsDone: Some Christians hear the blind man's cry, have mercy on me, in the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox Christians and others repeat, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; the story is also read when praying for healing and for spiritual sight.

fork.reveal: "he cried so much the more," and Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought, and asked: what wilt thou?

original.note: Greek: that I may see again. the verb can also mean to look up.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story about a blind man healed.
what it means: the blind man sees who Jesus is, shouts louder when hushed, and is asked what he wants, while the disciples with eyes understand nothing.
what a scholar hears: Luke sets the blind man straight after the disciples' failure to understand, and his son of David is a royal title on the road to Jerusalem.

notes: Carry 'jesus stood still' is the index line (lowercase as given); 'stood still' is Mark 10:49 KJV. Luke 18:40 KJV says 'Jesus stood'. The carry is kept exactly; the spoken carry capitalizes Jesus.
ἀναβλέπω: 'regain sight' and 'look up': standard lexicon. Confirm form ἀναβλέψω.
Year one (day 205, Bartimaeus) used Mark's version and the question 'what do you want?'; this day centers Luke's pairing with 18:34 and 'Jesus stood'.
The Jesus Prayer's link to Luke 18:38 and 18:13: commonly cited. Confirm.
